## How this course works this year {#ai-rule}

::: {.rule-line}
An AI assistant may write your code. **You must be able to check it.**
:::

::: {.duties}
::: {.duty}
[1 · Ask the right question]{.label}
State what you want to know and what the answer must look like: a number, its unit, its time window.
:::
::: {.duty}
[2 · Choose the treatment]{.label}
Decide what to do with missing values, repeats and outliers, and say why. The AI cannot know your plant.
:::
::: {.duty .key}
[3 · Verify the result]{.label}
Check row counts, units, ranges and one value by hand. Code that runs is not code that is right.
:::
:::

[The labs ask about 1, 2 and 3. None of them asks you to type code from memory.]{.note-line}

## 07:40, a file arrives {#incident}

::: {.logbook}
::: {.logrow}
[07:40]{.time} [A two-week export from a road-level air-quality station has arrived. The 09:00 report needs the mean CO concentration.]{.entry}
:::
::: {.logrow}
[07:55]{.time} [A colleague asks an AI assistant for code. It runs without an error and prints **−57.00 mg/m³**.]{.entry}
:::
:::

::: {.bridge}
A concentration cannot be negative. Nothing crashed, yet the number is wrong. Today is about catching this before it reaches the report.
:::

[Data: S. De Vito, Air Quality, UCI Machine Learning Repository, doi:10.24432/C59K5F, CC BY 4.0. The −57.00 is computed from one student's 14-day window.]{.source}

## What a plant data file contains {#anatomy}

| Timestamp | Tag | Value | Unit | Quality |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-01-07 13:00:00 | FI-101 | 12.4 | m³/h | good |
| 2026-01-07 13:00:01 | TI-205 | 78.3 | °C | good |
| 2026-01-07 13:00:02 | FI-101 | 0.0 | m³/h | bad: I/O timeout |
| 2026-01-07 14:00:00 | LAB-NH3 | 0.42 | wt% | lab, 1 per shift |

::: {.anatomy-notes}
[Timestamp]{.k} local or UTC? daylight saving? [Tag]{.k} which instrument, which unit operation. [Value + unit]{.k} the number means nothing without its unit. [Quality]{.k} the historian often says when a value is bad. A zero can be a reading or a failure.
:::

[Illustrative rows written for this slide; tag names follow common ISA practice.]{.source}

## Sampling rates do not agree {#sampling}

::: {.rates}
::: {.rate}
[Flow, pressure]{.label}
**1 s to 10 s**
Distributed control system
:::
::: {.rate}
[Temperature, level]{.label}
**10 s to 1 min**
Historian, often compressed
:::
::: {.rate}
[Hourly averages]{.label}
**1 h**
Environmental monitors, today's file
:::
::: {.rate .slow}
[Lab assay]{.label}
**1 per shift**
Sampled by hand, results hours later
:::
:::

::: {.bridge}
Joining a 1-second flow with a once-per-shift assay forces a choice: average, take the last value, or wait. Week 1, Lab 02 is about that choice.
:::

## Missing data wears many disguises {#codes}

::: {.disguises}
[empty cell]{.dz} [NaN]{.dz} [−200]{.dz .hit} [9999]{.dz} [−9999]{.dz} ["Bad"]{.dz} ["I/O Timeout"]{.dz} [0.0 during a trip]{.dz} [the same value for 6 hours]{.dz}
:::

::: {.bridge}
Rule: find how this file marks a missing value **before** you compute anything. Read the documentation, then confirm it in the data.
:::

[In today's file the source states that missing values are recorded as −200.]{.source}

## Activity 1 · Read the raw text {#act1 .activity}

[Pairs · 8 minutes · no computer]{.act-label}

```{=html}
<pre class="raw-lines"><span>Date;Time;CO(GT);PT08.S1(CO);NMHC(GT);C6H6(GT)</span><span>10/03/2004;18.00.00;2,6;1360;150;11,9</span><span>10/03/2004;19.00.00;2;1292;112;9,4</span><span>10/03/2004;20.00.00;2,2;1402;88;9,0</span><span>11/03/2004;04.00.00;-200;1011;14;1,3</span><span>12/03/2004;04.00.00;-200;831;10;1,1</span></pre>
```

::: {.prompt}
Write down four settings a program needs to read these lines correctly.
:::

[Hint: look at what separates the columns, what separates whole and decimal parts, how a missing CO reading looks, and how the date is written.]{.hint}

::: {.selfstudy}
Studying alone: write your four settings before you go to the next slide.
:::

## Activity 1 · The four settings {#act1-answer}

| Setting | In this file | If you get it wrong |
|---|---|---|
| Column separator | `;` | everything lands in one column |
| Decimal mark | `,` | 2,6 is read as text, no mean possible |
| Missing value | `-200` | −200 is averaged as a concentration |
| Date format | day/month/year, time `18.00.00` | 11/03 becomes 3 November |

[Both missing CO rows are at 04:00. Keep that in mind: missing values may follow a pattern. The Extension view of Lab 01 asks why.]{.note-line}

## The six-check audit {#audit}

::: {.six}
::: {.chk}
[1 · Shape]{.label}
Rows and columns as expected? 14 days of hourly data is 336 rows.
:::
::: {.chk}
[2 · Types]{.label}
Is every measurement a number, not text?
:::
::: {.chk}
[3 · Missing]{.label}
How many per column, in which code, at which times?
:::
::: {.chk}
[4 · Ranges and units]{.label}
Minimum and maximum physically possible? Units as documented?
:::
::: {.chk}
[5 · Repeats]{.label}
Any rows recorded twice?
:::
::: {.chk}
[6 · Time]{.label}
Does every step equal the sampling interval? Any jumps or repeats?
:::
:::

[Run all six before any mean, plot or model. They take minutes; a wrong report takes longer.]{.note-line}

## Reading code you did not write {#read-code}

```{=html}
<pre class="code-slide"><span><b class="c"># 1-2  shape and types</b></span><span>df = pd.read_csv("file.csv", sep=";", decimal=",", na_values=[-200])</span><span>df.shape                 <b class="c"># (rows, columns)</b></span><span>df.dtypes                <b class="c"># float64 = number, object = text</b></span><span><b class="c"># 3-4  missing and ranges</b></span><span>df.isna().sum()          <b class="c"># missing per column</b></span><span>df.describe()            <b class="c"># min, max, mean per column</b></span><span><b class="c"># 5-6  repeats and time</b></span><span>df.duplicated().sum()    <b class="c"># rows that repeat exactly</b></span><span>t.diff().value_counts()  <b class="c"># step sizes between timestamps</b></span></pre>
```

[You do not need to write these lines. You need to read them and say what each one tells you about the file.]{.note-line}

## Four ways to check code you did not write {#verify}

::: {.checks4}
::: {.c4}
[Count]{.label}
Rows before and after each step. If 3 rows vanish, you should know why.
:::
::: {.c4}
[Range]{.label}
Minimum and maximum against physics and units. A negative concentration is a bug.
:::
::: {.c4}
[Hand]{.label}
Compute one value from five rows by hand or on a calculator. Compare.
:::
::: {.c4}
[Look]{.label}
Plot before and after. A cleaning step should change the picture in the way you expect, and only there.
:::
:::

## Quick prediction: the AI's code {#ai-code}

```{=html}
<pre class="code-slide"><span>df = pd.read_csv("my_air_quality.csv", sep=";", decimal=",")</span><span>df = df.drop_duplicates()</span><span>print(df["CO(GT)"].mean())</span></pre>
```

::: {.prompt}
In a file where 99 of 336 CO hours are −200 and the valid hours average 2.74 mg/m³, what does this print? Estimate it in one minute.
:::

::: {.selfstudy}
Studying alone: estimate the number, then go on.
:::

## It prints −57.00 {#ai-answer}

::: {.calc}
(237 × 2.74 + 99 × (−200)) / 336 ≈ **−57.0 mg/m³**
:::

::: {.beforeafter}
::: {}
[What went wrong]{.label}
Separator and decimal mark are right, repeats are removed, but −200 is never declared missing. Every gap is averaged as a concentration.
:::
::: {}
[The fix, and the check]{.label}
Add `na_values=[-200]` when reading. Then check: missing count 99, minimum above zero, mean 2.74.
:::
:::

[A number can be wrong without an error message. The Range check catches this one in seconds.]{.note-line}
